newsitem.title: USA: Judge finds against PacBell ISDN rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Judge finds against PacBell ISDN rate rise.

text.p: A California administrative law judge has found Pacific Telesis's Pacific Bell unit has failed to justify its proposal to increase ISDN rates in the state, Intel Corp said in a statement.
California Public Utilities Commission administrative law Judge Kim Malcolm found numerous difficiencies in Pacific Bell's cost justifications for the planned rate hike, it said.

The ruling was made on Tuesday and parties which had participated actively in the matter, including Intel, Compaq Computer Corp and the Utility Consumer's Action Network (UCAN) were informed by mail of the decision.

Intel said it had joined with Compaq and UCAN in issuing the statement, noting the judge had recommended retaining the existing rate of $24.50 a month, rather than the $32.50 a month home ISDN rate requested by Pacific Bell.
Furthermore, the allowance for off-peak period usage would be 200 hours, instead of the 20-hour limit sought by the telecommuncations company, the statement said.
The decision is subject to further proceedings, but the two companies and the consumer group aid the judge's findings are expected to be endorsed by the full commission next month.

"The judge found that Pacific Bell's ISDN customer and installation service was unreasonable and inadequate, and adopted a variety of remedial incentives to ensure that Pacific Bell significantly improves its service by March 1997," the statement said.

The rollout of ISDN, or integrated services digital network, service in California has been controversial, with many people working in areas of the state's most concentrated high tech businesses demanding more accelerated service.
ISDN enables homes and small businesses to be connected to computer networks, such as the Internet, at several times the speed currently available using regular telephone lines.

Scott Smith, spokesman at Pacific Bell's data services group, said the rate proposal had not been conclusively struck down, however, saying the company was given 20 days to submit more data to the judge pending a possible further ruling.
The company intends to make a further submission, he said.
A spokesman for Intel said, however, that opponents of the increase did not expect the judge's current recommendations to be changed or overruled by the full commission.
"Our general experience has been that the commission generally agree with what the administrative law judge recommends in these sort of cases," said Intel spokesman Howard High.

"We believe that the core issues are solid, which is that we have a situation here where there really aren't other competitive economic alternatives to other ISDN service as a high bandwidth option for most residential and small business in PacBell's California region," he added.
"This is the best alternative, and this is in many cases the only alternative," High said. "We think it should be a 'grow the market' model and not a 'grow the price' model."
